conceptTag: The first 100 days of a juice bar
readerTitle: A juice bar's first 100 days: which number to watch, and who to ask
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주스 바, 온라인 요리 강좌) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 개업 초기에는 할 일을 늘리기보다, 숫자 하나를 정하고 매주 손님에게 그 숫자가 왜 움직이는지 물어보면 다음 할 일이 저절로 좁혀진다.
misconception: 매출이 떨어지면 가격을 내리거나 메뉴를 늘리는 것이 먼저다. 손님이 원하는 것을 모두 들어주면 된다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: ENT-05-02 (숫자 하나에 집중), ENT-05-03 (매주 손님과 대화)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 하루 판매 180잔 → 110잔, 2주 내 재방문 손님 약 5명 중 1명(20%) → 100일째 약 3명 중 1명(약 33%). 카드 간 수치가 일치하는지 다시 확인하세요.
출근길 손님이 기다릴 수 있는 시간 '약 3분', 실제 대기 '약 8분'은 가상 설정입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않도록 일러스트 라벨이 붙어 있는지 확인하세요.
온라인 요리 강좌 사례도 가상입니다. 수치를 쓰지 않고 상황만 설명했습니다.

cards.title: Opening week was a hit. Day 30 was quiet.
body: Maya opens a juice bar near a train station. Opening week, she sells about 180 cups a day. Friends come, neighbors come, a local blog posts photos.
By day 30, she's down to 110. She has 70 days of savings left before she needs a new plan, and a list of twenty ideas to try.

image.label: A small juice bar counter with a half-empty morning line
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 역 앞 작은 주스 바 카운터, 아침 햇살. 카운터 위 벽에 포스트잇 20장이 빼곡히 붙어 있고 사장이 그것을 바라보며 고민하는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which number should Maya watch every day?
body: She can only track one thing well while running the counter. Which number tells her most about whether the juice bar will last?

options.feedback: It matters, but it mixes curious first-timers with loyal regulars. It tells her sales fell, not why.

options.text: Share of new customers who come back within two weeks
options.feedback: This is **focusing on one number**. A station juice bar lives on repeat commuters, and this number shows whether she's building them.

options.text: Followers on her social media account
options.feedback: Easy to grow and nice to see. But followers don't pay rent, and they can rise while the counter stays empty.

cards.title: Only about 1 in 5 came back.
body: Maya adds a simple stamp card with a date on it. After two weeks, the cards tell a clear story: only about **1 in 5** new customers returned within 14 days.
Now her twenty ideas look different. A new flavor, a loyalty discount or a bigger sign might bring more first-timers. None of them obviously fixes why people don't come back.
The number didn't give her the answer. It told her which question to ask.

cards.title: Twenty minutes at the counter, every Monday.
body: Maya starts **talking to customers every week**. Each Monday morning, she asks five people one question: what almost stopped you from coming today? She also texts a few people whose stamp cards went quiet.
The answers repeat. Commuters love the juice. But at the morning peak, the wait is about eight minutes, and they have about three before their train.

image.label: Owner chatting with a commuter across the counter, a clock showing rush hour
image.brief: 카운터 너머로 사장이 출근길 손님과 짧게 이야기하는 장면. 손님은 손목시계를 보고 있고, 벽시계는 오전 8시 근처. 사장 손에 작은 메모장. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three complaints. Which one first?
body: Customers mention three things: prices feel high, the morning wait is long, and they'd like more flavors. Maya can fix one this month.

options.text: Cut prices by 15% to win people back
options.feedback: It answers the loudest complaint but costs money on every cup. And the people who left mostly blamed the wait, not the price.

options.text: Bottle the three best-sellers before 7 a.m. for a grab-and-go shelf
options.feedback: It targets what lapsed customers actually said, and her one number will show within two weeks whether it worked. Talking and measuring check each other.

options.text: Add four new flavors to keep things fresh
options.feedback: Fans may enjoy it, but more choices could make the morning line even slower.

cards.title: Fewer ideas, better results.
body: The grab-and-go shelf sells out most mornings. By day 100, about **1 in 3** new customers comes back within two weeks. Daily sales climb back without a single discount.
Maya's list of twenty ideas is still on the wall. She has tried two. The number and the Monday conversations told her which two mattered.

cards.title: Both tools can fool you.
body: One number can hide trouble. If returns rise while each cup loses money, the number looks great while the savings shrink. Glance at cash, even when you focus on one thing.
Customers can mislead too. People often say *price* when they mean something else. Trust what they did, like the dates on a stamp card, over what they say they'd do.
And the right number changes. After day 100, Maya may need to watch something new.

cards.title: Now it's an online cooking course.
body: Sam launched a paid video cooking course two months ago. Sign-ups were strong at launch, then slowed. Sam has time for one weekly habit. Which plan fits best?

options.text: Track weekly sign-ups and spend the time on ads
options.feedback: Sign-ups are like Maya's opening-week crowd. They can hide that buyers stop after one video, and ads just pour more people into the same leak.

options.text: Track how many buyers finish lesson two, and each week email five who stopped
options.feedback: One number that shows real use, plus weekly conversations with people who drifted away. Together they point to what to fix first.

options.text: Survey all buyers once about which new recipes they want
options.feedback: It's listening, but once and to everyone. The people who quit early hold the most useful answers, and new recipes may not be why they left.

cards.title: Pick one number. Ask why it moves.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **Focus on one number** showed Maya where the problem was. **Talking to customers every week** showed her why. Each kept the other honest.
**Try it today:** write down the one number that best shows whether your customers come back. Then ask three people this week what almost stopped them.
